findings.description: No test in the suite exercises a `"**"` field spec resolving onto a scalar-valued field through a non-empty path prefix (e.g. `"contact.email.**"` where `email` is a string). The only `"**"` tests are `project(data, ["contact.**"])` (an object target, line 90-92) and root-level `project(data, ["**"])` (line 126-129) — the latter short-circuits at `FieldPath.ts`'s very first line of `projectAt` (`tails.some(tail.length===1 && tail[0]==="**") return value`) before ever recursing into a child, so it never touches the recursive branch at FieldPath.ts:186 where a `"**"` tail is handed to `projectAt` for an individual child value via `deeper.get(key)`. A grep across `packages/core/test/*.ts` confirms `"**"` is used nowhere outside this file, so the recursive-scalar case is untested project-wide, not just in this file.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a case like `project({ contact: { email: "a@b.com" } }, ["contact.email.**"])` asserting the whole scalar is returned, exercising the recursive `"**"` branch rather than only the root-level short-circuit.

findings.description: The comment says "All fourteen variants have an arm, so all fourteen need exercising", but the `leaves` array immediately below it (lines 75-86) lists exactly 10 policies, matching the Policy ADT's actual 10 leaf tags (HasPermission, HasRole, HasAttribute, HasResourceAttribute, HasRelationship, HasAction, HasActed, HasNotActed, HasCustom, HasSignature — confirmed against Policy.ts's tag union). The full ADT has 16 tags total (10 leaves + 6 composites: AllOf, AnyOf, Not, Labeled, Obliged, Rules), so "fourteen" matches neither the leaf count nor the total. The test itself is complete (all 10 real leaves are exercised); only the number in the comment is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Change "fourteen" to "ten" (or otherwise correct the count) so the comment matches the array it describes.

findings.description: `SecurityLabel.ts`'s `LabelOrdering` (`"Equal" | "Dominates" | "DominatedBy" | "Incomparable"`) and `FieldPath.ts`'s `Containment` (`"Equal" | "ALessB" | "BLessA" | "Incomparable"`, FieldPath.ts:85) are both four-valued results of a partial-order comparison function in the same package, but use two different naming schemes for the non-Equal/non-Incomparable pair — one semantic (Dominates/DominatedBy), one positional (ALessB/BLessA). `FieldPath.ts`'s own doc comment (lines 82-84) explains the positional choice for its domain, so this isn't necessarily wrong, but a reader moving between the two sibling comparison APIs sees inconsistent vocabulary for the same shape of result.
findings.suggestedFix: No fix required; noted for awareness. If a third partial-order type is ever added, consider settling on one naming convention (semantic vs. positional) across the package, or documenting why the two differ.
